We consider a frozen vision backbone Φ\Phi composed of LL layers, used as a feature extractor. For notational simplicity, we omit the sample index ii when it is clear from context. Given a training image xx, the backbone outputs a sequence of intermediate representations Φ⁡(x)=(h(1),h(2),…,h(L))\Phi(x)=\bigl(h^{(1)},h^{(2)},\ldots,h^{(L)}\bigr), where h(ℓ)∈ℝdh^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the layer-ℓ\ell [CLS] token (dd is the embedding dimension), used as a compact global descriptor of layer ℓ\ell. Collecting all [CLS] tokens over the training set yields a feature tensor ℋ∈ℝN×L×d\mathcal{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times L\times d}, exposing the full representational hierarchy across depth. In contrast to standard practice, which typically relies only on the final layer, our goal is to exploit information across layers.

The recoverability analysis shows that intermediate ViT layers contain corrective signals distributed across depth, but not in the form of independent ensemble diversity. This motivates VFusion: a lightweight mechanism that treats the layer hierarchy as a redundant yet informative representation trace and compresses selected frozen features into a compact task-specific latent token. Figure 2 illustrates the proposed framework, which consists of three components. Layer selection chooses a subset of layers from the frozen backbone. Layer fusion concatenates their representations and compresses them into a single global token via a learnable fusion encoder. Supervised training jointly learns the fusion encoder and a lightweight classifier head while keeping the backbone parameters fixed. We describe each component below.

The vertical scope of the fusion manifold is defined by selecting a subset of layers 𝒮⊆{1,…,L}\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{1,\dots,L\} of size MM. We consider three selection strategies to balance computational cost and corrective signal diversity: (i) holistic, utilizing the full depth (M=LM=L) to preserve the complete information trace; (ii) last-half (𝒮={L/2,…,L}\mathcal{S}=\{L/2,\dots,L\}) to focus on the deepest part of the network, and (iii) strided (𝒮={2,4,6,…}\mathcal{S}=\{2,4,6,\dots\}) (up to LL) to reduce dimensionality while maintaining coverage across depth.

Given a selected subset of layers 𝒮\mathcal{S}, our objective is to aggregate their representations into a single global token that consolidates complementary information distributed across depth. Our layer-wise analysis (cf. Table 1, Figure 1) shows that intermediate layers frequently correct mistakes made by the final layer, with recoverability strongly correlated with correction entropy. Importantly, this recoverability is not explained by geometric disagreement between logits, suggesting that complementarity arises from distributed conditional correction capacity rather than from purely divergent predictions. These findings motivate aggregation mechanisms that consolidate cross-layer corrective signals instead of selecting a single “best” layer.

We interpret each layer representation h(ℓ)h^{(\ell)} as containing a task-relevant component s(ℓ)∈ℝds^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a task-irrelevant component r(ℓ)∈ℝdr^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}: h(ℓ)=s(ℓ)+r(ℓ)h^{(\ell)}=s^{(\ell)}+r^{(\ell)}, where ℓ∈𝒮\ell\in\mathcal{S} represents the respective layer and dd the embedding dimension. Under this model, multiple layers provide distinct but potentially overlapping task-relevant information.

Concatenating the selected features yields a single vector

v=[h(ℓ)]ℓ∈𝒮∈ℝM⋅d,v=\big[\,h^{(\ell)}\,\big]_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\cdot d}, (6)

which enables a fusion model to explicitly access all relevant information, even if a specific piece of it was available in intermediate layers before being transformed into more complex but task-irrelevant information.

We introduce a learnable fusion encoder

ℰ:ℝM⋅d→ℝdz,z=ℰ⁡(v),z∈ℝdz,\mathcal{E}:\mathbb{R}^{M\cdot d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}},\quad z=\mathcal{E}(v),\quad z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}, (7)

which maps the concatenated multi-layer feature vector vv into a low-dimensional latent zz with dz≪M⋅dd_{z}\ll M\cdot d, and applies LayerNorm to produce an approximately standard-normalized latent. By imposing this low-dimensional representation, the encoder acts as a noise-suppression filter that discards layer-specific residuals r(ℓ)r^{(\ell)} to isolate the task-relevant signal ss shared across the representational hierarchy. In practice, ℰ\mathcal{E} is implemented as a multi-layer perceptron with non-linear activations, enabling flexible interactions across layers and allowing the fusion encoder to learn non-trivial cross-depth dependencies. Under this formulation, layer fusion becomes a supervised cross-layer dimensionality reduction problem: the encoder learns how to align and compress complementary evidence distributed across intermediate representations into a single global token suitable for downstream prediction. This avoids committing to any single layer and instead leverages the distributed correction capacity observed empirically in Table 1.
ℰ:ℝM⋅d→ℝdz,z=ℰ⁡(v),z∈ℝdz,\mathcal{E}:\mathbb{R}^{M\cdot d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}},\quad z=\mathcal{E}(v),\quad z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}, (7)

Given the fused latent representation z=ℰ⁡(v)∈ℝdzz=\mathcal{E}(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}, we attach a lightweight classifier Γ:ℝdz→ℝ|𝒴|\Gamma:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{Y}|} that maps the compact global token to class logits 𝐲^=Γ⁡(z)\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\Gamma(z). The fusion encoder ℰ\mathcal{E} and classifier Γ\Gamma are trained jointly under supervised classification loss, while the backbone Φ\Phi remains frozen throughout.

Inspired by redundancy-reduction objectives [54, 3], we mitigate redundancy in the fused latent representation by introducing a decorrelation regularizer that penalizes linear dependencies across dimensions. While the low-dimensional projection imposes a strong inductive bias for information compression, it does not explicitly prevent different latent dimensions from encoding redundant features. We compare VFusion against several layer-aggregation baselines, treating each intermediate layer representation as an independent expert. Non-parametric methods combine layer-wise predictions without learning additional parameters: probability averaging (Average), majority voting (Majority), and selecting the best-performing individual layer (Best layer). Parametric methods learn combinations of layer-wise outputs. Super Learner (SL) [24] learns a fixed linear combination of layer predictors, whereas the Neural Logit Controller (NLC) [44] performs input-dependent calibration by predicting temperature-scaling parameters for the layer experts. Feature-based routing methods operate on the concatenated feature representation, including sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) [46] and Switch-MoE (sw-MoE) [11]. For a fair comparison, MoE and sw-MoE receive the same concatenated features as VFusion. MoE uses top-kk routing (k=4k=4), while sw-MoE is the hard-routing case (k=1k=1).

We define all classification heads Γ\Gamma as MLPs with hidden dimension 128128, optimized with Adam under cross-entropy loss. We train with batch size 512512 for up to 20,00020{,}000 iterations, and apply early stopping based on validation loss evaluated every 500500 iterations: training stops if the loss does not decrease by at least 10−410^{-4} for 55 consecutive evaluations, and we retain the checkpoint with the best validation loss. The backbone remains frozen throughout. For layer-wise probes, we select hyperparameters on a held-out validation set via a per-layer grid search over learning rate {10−4,10−3,10−2,10−1}\{10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1}\} and weight decay {0,10−3,10−2}\{0,10^{-3},10^{-2}\}. For MoE, we set the number of experts to MM and a learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} [44]. For VFusion, we set the latent dimension to dz=256d_{z}=256 and the orthogonalization weight to λ=2.0\lambda=2.0. The encoder ℰ\mathcal{E} is a 33-layer MLP with widths [2048,1024,512][2048,1024,512] and output dimension 256256. We train (ℰ,Γ)(\mathcal{E},\Gamma) with learning rate 10−410^{-4} and weight decay 10−310^{-3}. Unless stated otherwise, we adopt the holistic layer-selection strategy. All results are averaged over three seed runs.

We next test whether the same feature-level fusion principle extends from vertical aggregation within a model to horizontal aggregation across models. Using the three ViT-B backbones introduced above, IN21k, DINOv2, and CLIP, we treat each backbone as an expert. For logit-level baselines (Average, Majority, SL, NLC), we train an MLP probe on each backbone’s last-layer features and aggregate the resulting predictions. Feature-level methods, namely sw-MoE and HFusion, instead operate on the concatenated last-layer features from the three backbones. Since the ensemble contains only three experts, we omit sparse MoE and report sw-MoE with k=1k{=}1. Finally, VFusion denotes vertical fusion within the strongest single backbone, DINOv2, using holistic layer selection, whereas HFusion denotes horizontal fusion across the three backbones.

While VFusion demonstrates substantial performance gains, the fusion encoder currently requires supervision to learn a task-specific aggregation of the feature representations. Future work could explore how to learn such a latent space in unsupervised or self-supervised regimes, potentially enabling large-scale fusion pre-training without the need for labeled data.

Furthermore, layer selection is currently based on simple, predefined strategies rather than being learned jointly with the fusion encoder. We also evaluate VFusion primarily in the frozen-backbone setting. Studying how vertical fusion interacts with partial or full fine-tuning remains an important direction.
Lastly, we evaluate VFusion only for supervised classification. Future work can adapt vertical fusion to other computer vision tasks, including dense prediction (e.g., segmentation).

We next test whether VFusion’s gains come from intermediate-layer information rather than added module capacity. We introduce a capacity-controlled Final-only baseline with the same Enc+LN+Head architecture and training protocol as VFusion, but using only the final-layer representation h(L)h^{(L)} as input.

As shown in Table C2, VFusion consistently outperforms this capacity-matched baseline on average (91.4%91.4\% vs. 90.7%90.7\%). The difference is small on saturated datasets, where both methods already approach ceiling performance, but becomes pronounced on less-saturated benchmarks. In particular, VFusion notably improves over Final-only on GTS (+4.3%+4.3\%), FGVC (+4.2%+4.2\%), Cars (+1.2%+1.2\%), and PC (+0.8%+0.8\%). These results indicate that the gains observed in previous experiments are not merely due to a larger classifier head, but arise from fusing complementary information distributed across intermediate layers.
